name: Beth Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 27. I live with my partner Ryan in a little rented cottage on Church Lane, he's an apprentice mechanic at the garage in town. I work at Meridian, they make vitamins and supplements, I've been on the tablet presses there about six months. And on the side I make candles and sell them online, which is my baby, really.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a tablet press, which squeezes powder into tablets, thousands a minute. I check the weight and hardness every fifteen minutes and write it in the batch record, and if the weight drifts I have to adjust it, which I still get wrong sometimes, so Mrs. Patel the senior operator double-checks me. The worst part is the cleaning between batches, everything comes apart and you scrub it in a gown and mask for two hours. But it's careful work, I like that, and the chatbot on my phone has been brilliant for helping me understand the batch paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still a brilliant tool, people just expected too much. I'd tell the girls at work to use it anyway, it writes all my candle descriptions. Online I'd probably post something cheerful about how it's still useful for small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes very little for me. Meridian's already got some automation and my job's about the same either way. I'd keep using the AI every day for the candle shop and for learning the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the presses and aim to be signed off on my own by the new year. I'd grow the candle shop, maybe add a wax melt range for Christmas, which could bring in an extra hundred or two a month. That would go straight into savings, because we've got about three weeks of bills put by and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit busy, but happy busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the candle shop start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: During a bad winter two years ago, I was out of work for a bit, and my grandma taught me how to pour candles the way she did. I asked the AI how to set up a shop online and how to price things, and I sold my first twenty to people from church. Now I sell maybe forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your savings are about three weeks. How does that feel day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight but not scary, if that makes sense. We don't spend much, Ryan fixes our car himself and we eat at his mum's on Sundays. If something big went, his family would help, and I'd pay them back.

S0.say: She'd say AI is still a brilliant tool and people just expected too much, and would tell co-workers to use it. Online she'd post about how useful it remains for small businesses.
S0.think: She thinks it changes very little for her factory job. She'd keep using AI every day for her candle shop and to learn batch paperwork.
S0.do: Works towards being signed off on the tablet press by the new year and adds a wax melt range for Christmas, which could bring in an extra one or two hundred a month. Puts that extra straight into savings, currently about three weeks of bills.
S0.quote: I asked the AI how to set up a shop online and how to price things, and I sold my first twenty to people from church.
S0.fieldNote: Beth blends old family skills with daily AI use, and her side business matters to her as much as the factory job. A plateau costs her nothing. Her safety net is her partner's family, not the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing if people take responsibility and learn. At work I'd say get comfortable with the new systems, don't wait for someone to hold your hand. I'd post about how AI helped me start a business from my kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's mostly good for me. Meridian will bring in more automated presses, and they'll want people who can run the software and do the checks, and I pick things up fast. And the candle shop gets easier, not harder, with better tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask to train on the new automated press line as soon as it arrives, and I'd use the AI to study the manuals and the regulations for medicine-making. I'd look into a part-time quality course at the college, so I could move into checking and approving batches, which pays better. And I'd put a few hundred from the candle money into a second wax melter, so I can double my output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs. Patel, maybe. She's brilliant on the old presses, but she doesn't trust computers. I'd offer to show her the new screens, quietly, so she doesn't feel shown up by a junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should take responsibility. Does anyone else have a part to play?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies should train their own people, that's just good business, it's cheaper than hiring. And families should back each other up. I don't think it's the government's job to retrain everyone, but I'd not turn away a free course if it was there.

S1.say: She'd say it's good if people take responsibility and learn, urging co-workers to get comfortable with new systems without waiting to be led. She'd post about starting a business from her kitchen table with AI's help.
S1.think: She thinks it's mostly good for her, since automated presses will need fast learners to run software and checks. Better tools would make her candle shop easier too.
S1.do: Asks to train on the new automated press line and studies manuals and regulations with AI. Looks into a part-time quality course to move into batch checking and invests a few hundred from candle sales in a second wax melter.
S1.feel: Pretty good, like a door opening.
S1.quote: I'd offer to show her the new screens, quietly, so she doesn't feel shown up by a junior.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change reads as opportunity to her on both fronts, the factory and her business. Her traditional view puts training on companies and families, though she's pragmatic about a free course. She thinks carefully about an older colleague's pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after their own and their neighbours, because no government is going to be ready for that. I'd say keep faith and keep working at whatever you can. I'd try to sound steady, even if I wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be really worried. My factory job would go, and Ryan's too, because a robot that can do anything can fix a car. And my candles only sell because people have a bit of spare money, and if everyone's out of work, nobody's buying a fancy candle for twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away, and stop buying stock for the shop beyond what's already ordered. I'd switch the candles to cheaper basics and sell at the church fair and the market, not just online. If we lost both jobs, we'd move in with Ryan's mum and dad, they've got the room, and I'd do anything for cash, cleaning, caring, whatever's still going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly. Like I'd built a little boat and the sea just dried up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned nobody buying a fancy candle for twenty. Is there anything people would still pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe things made by someone you know. My grandma always said people pay for a face, not a product. But that's a guess, and if people haven't got money, a face doesn't help much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was there and everyone was getting it, probably, yes. It wouldn't be a handout if the whole country is in the same boat, it'd be more like flood relief. But I'd want to be working at something, even if it's small.

S2.say: She'd say people must look after their own and their neighbours because no government would be ready, and urge keeping faith and working at whatever is available. She'd try to sound steady.
S2.think: She'd be really worried: both her job and her partner's mechanic job would go, and her candles depend on people having spare money. If everyone is out of work, nobody buys a fancy candle for twenty.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, stops buying shop stock and switches to cheaper candles sold at church fairs and markets. If both jobs go, moves in with her partner's parents and takes any cash work, such as cleaning or care.
S2.feel: Scared, like a little boat left on a dried-up sea.
S2.quote: My candles only sell because people have a bit of spare money, and if everyone's out of work, nobody's buying a fancy candle for twenty.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability gives her ideas, but she sees clearly that her side business depends on other people's wages. She accepts government help if it's universal, likening it to flood relief. She'd keep a steady public face while privately afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ready if you're sensible, so be sensible. Save, learn, help your family. At work I'd say get on the new systems now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32. I think the quality job would last a few years, maybe till near the end, and I'd have time to build the candle shop into something real, maybe with a little unit. But I'd know the clock was running, and I'd want money in the bank by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the quality course in the first year and move into batch release, which is the person who signs off that a batch is safe. I'd use AI to run the shop's orders and stock, so it takes less of my evenings, and aim for a hundred candles a month. Every bit of extra money would go into savings, so we've got six months put by before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a busy, hopeful way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at home change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ryan and I want to get married, probably in the next couple of years. I wouldn't put that off, if anything I'd want it sooner, family's what gets you through. But we might wait on children until we know where the money's coming from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use AI to run the shop. Isn't that the same thing that's coming for the jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know, it's funny. But it's a tool, like a sewing machine was for my grandma. The difference is whether you own it or it owns you, and in my shop, I own it.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough if people are sensible: save, learn and help family. At work she'd urge everyone onto the new systems now.
S3.think: She expects the quality job to last a few years and to have time to grow her candle shop, maybe into a small unit. She'd feel the clock running and want savings by the end.
S3.do: Takes the quality course in year one and moves into batch release, signing off batches as safe. Uses AI to run shop orders and stock, aims for a hundred candles a month and saves every extra towards six months of bills.
S3.quote: It's a tool, like a sewing machine was for my grandma. The difference is whether you own it or it owns you, and in my shop, I own it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her build two tracks, a better factory role and a real small business. She sees no contradiction in using AI while it threatens jobs, framing it as ownership. She'd marry sooner but wait on children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so there's no reason not to get ready. Learn something, start something, look after your family. I'd say it cheerfully, because I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well for most of it, honestly. I'd be in quality at Meridian, the candle shop would be a proper little business, and we'd have savings. The end still worries me because of the customers, but I'd have years to work something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the quality course over the next year or two and move into batch release. I'd grow the shop slowly, maybe rent a small unit in year three and take on a helper, and use AI and a pouring machine to do more with less. I'd put money into the business and into savings, half and half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a little worry at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end worries you because of the customers. Can you explain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, a business is only as good as the people buying. If AGI takes everyone's job in 2036, my customers go with it. So I'd want by then to sell to people who'll still have money, or have a cushion big enough to ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said family's what gets you through. How does that fit with your plans for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it to be a family thing, really. Ryan could do the deliveries and fix the machines, maybe his sister would help with the packing. That way whatever happens, it's ours, and we're in it together.

S4.say: She'd call ten years a gift and say there's no reason not to get ready by learning, starting something and looking after family. She'd say it cheerfully and mean it.
S4.think: She expects to do well for most of the decade, in quality at Meridian with a proper small business and savings. The end worries her only because her customers might lose their incomes.
S4.do: Takes the quality course and moves into batch release over the next year or two. Grows the shop slowly, renting a small unit and taking on a helper around year three, using AI and a pouring machine, and splits spare money between the business and savings.
S4.feel: Mostly hopeful, with a little worry in the background.
S4.quote: A business is only as good as the people buying. If AGI takes everyone's job in 2036, my customers go with it.
S4.fieldNote: A decade lets her build a family business, which fits both her traditional values and her appetite for new tools. She spots a risk others might miss: her customers' incomes. Her plans are concrete and staged by year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. It takes my job, Ryan's job and my customers all at once. What would help is companies giving people notice and training, and if it's everyone at once, some help to tide families over, like you'd get after a flood.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people's small things on the side. Half the women on my shift sell something, cakes, nails, crochet. If the factory goes, that's what we'll lean on, and nobody counts it.

headlineQuote: My grandma always said people pay for a face, not a product.
portrait: Beth Young is a 27-year-old tablet press operator at a vitamin factory who runs a small online candle shop, a skill her grandmother taught her and AI helped her turn into a business. She uses AI every day and sees steady change as a door opening, planning to move into quality control and grow the shop. Fast AGI alarms her because it would take her job, her partner's job and her customers' spending money at once. With five or ten years she maps out staged plans for a family-run business and savings. Her views are traditional, putting responsibility on companies and families, though she'd accept universal help in a crisis.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take her job, her partner's job and her customers all at once.
whatWouldHelp: Companies giving notice and training, and if everyone is hit at once, temporary help for families like flood relief.
